speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1950-51 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been the practice in previous years to table the estimates and move that they be referred to the committee of supply without any explanatory statement in this house. My predecessor as minister and I have usually sent a brief explanatory statement to the press immediately after tabling the estimates. This year, in response to various suggestions, I propose to make a brief explanatory statement to the house itself when presenting the estimates.
It will be observed that the total of the estimates being proposed for the new fiscal year commencing April 1 is $2,308 million. This includes those items for which continuing statutory authority for the expenditure is already available-a total of $1,011 million- as well as the 560 votes for expenditure which we are putting before this house for its approval, and which add up to $1,297 million. In addition, we are proposing votes for loans and investments which will create active assets and which total $105 million. These are, of course, not included in the expenditure totals.
First, I wish to indicate how these figures compare with those for the current fiscal year now drawing to its close in March. As usual, we have shown throughout the estimates the comparable figures for the votes already passed by the house this past year, including supplementary estimates made to date, and the forecasts of statutory expenditure placed before the house with the estimates last year. These add up to $2,335 million-which is about $27 million more than the estimates now presented for the new year.
It is difficult to determine what past figures make a satisfactory comparison with those

maintopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1950-51 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I be permitted to make a suggestion which I hope will find some favour in connection with consideration of the estimates? It is not a new suggestion, and I hope the government, having considered the matter from previous sessions, will be agreeable to following it, at any rate to some extent.

Main Estimates
In the past we have been pursuing a rather irregular course in connection with the estimates. Some departments are brought in1 day-after day, while other departments are not touched until the last. My suggestion is that this session we try to find an orderly way of dealing with the estimates so that they may all be covered on something like an equal basis.
I am going to suggest to the Prime Minister that the house devote one day a week to estimates, and that each week the estimates of a new department be introduced. Having in mind the normal length of a session, we would reach the later part of the session with all departments dealt with although they might not be completed.
I think this would meet public desire, because no one could then say that parliament had not given all the estimates fair consideration as they went through. Of course toward the end of the session a number of matters would still require to be examined; nevertheless the examination of estimates would be spread over the entire field, something which, to the knowledge of all of us, has not been done for the past number of sessions.
I make this suggestion in perfectly good faith, in the hope that we may be able to establish a custom and practice in the House of Commons that not only will meet public favour but will prove of great convenience to the government and to parliament in general.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Acting Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: EXTENSION OF COVERAGE IN THE LUMBERING AND LOGGING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to table, for the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), P.C. 474. In connection with this order in council I wish to announce that the government is making an extension of unemployment insurance coverage in the lumbering and logging industry. With this important step about 75,000 workers in industry will receive the protection of unemployment insurance.
It will be recalled that the exclusion of lumbering and logging in the 1940 act was due mainly to the difficulty of administration. The chief difficulties were:
(1)	the seasonality of the industry in most
parts of Canada except on the west coast;
(2)	the inaccessible location of some of the
operations;
(3)	the high turnover of employees;
(4)	the large amount of subcontracting, and
(5)	the large number of farmers, fishermen
and other non-insured persons who work in logging camps for very short periods.
Initially attention was directed towards the establishment of the over-all insurance scheme, and later, after experience had been gained from the operation of that program, questions of extending the coverage to some of the excepted occupations received consideration in the light of newly-gained experience.
Both the unemployment insurance commission and the unemployment insurance advisory committee have for several years given a great deal of study to the advisability of and ways and means of extending coverage to this industry.
In 1946 employees in lumbering and logging in the province of British Columbia were brought under insurable employment. The government insured lumbering and logging in British Columbia because in that province it is an all-year-round industry, whereas in other parts of Canada the seasonal factor is important. Further, it was considered that it would be useful to gain some experience in one area in Canada before extending coverage to other areas.
Since this time the advisory committee and the commission have reviewed the question of further extensions, and the commission has held public hearings. Every effort has

been made to obtain workable provision for the coverage of those employees in the industry who require protection.
As a result of full investigation of the many phases of the industry it has been decided that seasonal regulations under the Unemployment Insurance Act will apply to the industry except in British Columbia, where of course they are now in an insurable state.
This means those people whose only insurable employment is in lumbering and logging can draw benefits only during the logging season. In the prairies this season is for the time being regarded as from November 1 to April 15, and in eastern Canada, from November 1 to March 31. However, people who are employed in lumbering and logging during part of the year and in other insurable employments during the remainder of the year, even to a limited extent, are not affected by the seasonal regulations, which are designed to exclude from benefit in the off-season only those whose employment is seasonal.
Provision has also been made for the voluntary exclusion from coverage of farmers, hunters, fishermen, and others whose main employment is not insurable when these persons do not expect to work in lumbering and logging for more than sixty days in any year. It would be unfair to take unemployment contributions from persons who would be unable to obtain sufficient contributions to qualify for benefit. Accordingly this exclusion is voluntary to allow flexibility that might be needed in certain cases but in the main only affects those whose contributions from their work in this industry would not be sufficient to give them benefits under the act.
Up to the present time certain planing mills and saw mills which work only part of the year have been excluded. These saw mills will also be brought under insurance coverage.
April 1 has been set as the date of commencement of these new provisions, because it is thought to be the most suitable date to begin contribution collections. It comes at a time when employers in the industry will not be in the position of having to apply the regulations to their employees when their payroll staff is overloaded with work. Since insurance books are renewed each year on April 1, it will be an advantage to issue books for the new insurance year 1950-51 rather than to issue books at an earlier date for the current fiscal year, which would have to be renewed shortly afterwards.
Unemployment Insurance
These coverage provisions have been carefully adapted to the particular needs of the industry. As I mentioned yesterday in this house, our seasonal trends are, because of our climatic conditions, more pronounced than in other countries, and we believe we should shape our insurance scheme as far as practicable to take these conditions into account. This extension of insurance coverage to lumbering and logging in parts of Canada where the industry is highly seasonal will bring to these workers the protection they need and deserve against the hazards of unemployment. The broadening of coverage under this measure is another important advance in the development of a more comprehensive insurance program as a first line of defence for workers and their families against unemployment.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (for the Minister of Labour) moved
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 8, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to make a few observations on the motion for second reading, though most matters were dealt with yesterday in>
the discussion of the resolution.
Before beginning my general remarks in this connection I feel that mention should be made of the general regret on the part of all hon. members, irrespective of where they sit in this house, at the fact that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) is indisposed and unable himself to move second reading. If there is one member or minister in this house who enjoys the friendship of all-and after all, that is the way it should be in parliament -it is the Minister of Labour. We all trust that very shortly he will be back in the house discharging his responsibilities.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It will interest the hon. member if I say that yesterday I received an encouraging letter from the Minister of Labour. I hope, as my hon. friend does, that within a very short time the minister will return to the house in his usual good health.

And saying things, as he always does, in so kindly a manner.
It was only about half an hour ago, Mr. Speaker, that my hon. friend the acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) asked me to say a few words on the question of unemployment insurance. In the interval I looked up the representations and recommendations made by the Sirois commission, as well as those made by the dominion government to the dominion-provincial conference of 1945. When one reads those recommendations it is difficult to understand what happened to them; for the extent to which they have been adopted is so infinitesimal, as compared with what was sought by those representations, that it seems beyond comprehension that there should' have been any controversy at all in the matter.
The Sirois commission recommended that the dominion should be responsible for the employable unemployed. The bill now before us, as was said yesterday, effective though it may be as far as it goes, omits so many things, having regard to present conditions, that in the opinion of the opposition it is most inadequate to meet the unemployment situation of today. I go back to 1945; I am going

to read a tew of the recommendations made at that time by members of the government, with a view to offering certain suggestions with respect to further amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. As I see it, on this motion for second reading not only are we discussing the general principle of the bill; we are also discussing the situation facing this country today, the whole matter of unemployment.
At page 6 of the report of proceedings of the 1945' conference, the then prime minister said:
We are convinced that the people of Canada expect governments-all governments-to accept responsibility for creating conditions which will ensure high and stable employment. To create such conditions, we believe it should be made possible, through reduction and simplification of taxes, and in other ways, for private enterprise to operate boldly and courageously.
I pause here to say that at that time the then prime minister particularly mentioned that in order to encourage employment it was necessary to reduce taxation. Then he went on to say:
We believe the state-and by the state, may I say again, I mean provinces as well as dominion- should design programs of public development and conservation which can be readily expanded or contracted to help in balancing the rise and fall of other sources of employment.
I point this out because, as was suggested yesterday, I feel that many unemployed people in this dominion will not be covered by the Unemployment Insurance Act as it now stands, or even with these suggested amendments. There are many excepted employments; there are many casual workers. But if they be unemployed, no matter what their classification, they demand and deserve help at this time. I referred to public works. The present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) did so as well at pages 55 to 60 of the proceedings, when he said:
The purpose should not be to find a "cure-all" for unemployment in huge expenditures on public works. Rather, the problem is one of devising a sound and consistent program of public improvements-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext:
All or at least some of these recommendations were made at the dominion-provincial conference of 1945. At that time it was suggested that the question of unemployment should be faced in a certain way. In a moment I am coming to what the Minister of Labour had to say on that occasion. He provided for alternatives first in the Unemployment Insurance Act, and then in provision for those who are employable but are unemployed. He asserted that they were the responsibility of the federal authority. Finally the minister made certain suggestions as to increasing the ambit of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
What I am doing is discussing the principle at issue here. As the member has said, the purpose of the measure now proposed is to meet the situation prevailing today. We in the opposition say that, as far as it goes, it will meet part of the situation, but it cannot provide for the more than 100,000 unemployed who do not come within the ambit of the Unemployment Insurance Act. It is for this reason, sir, that I am discussing the recommendations of 1945. I trust that I may be permitted to continue, even though a reading of the promises made by the members of the government in 1945 indicates that many of those promises have fallen into the limbo of things forgotten and unperformed. I await your ruling, sir.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: It is rather difficult to determine just what is the principle of the amending bill before the house. I do feel, however, that it has to do with the bringing of additional workers within the provisions of the present act, known as the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940. I do not see any provisions in the bill which provide for creating employment.
That is the trouble with it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: That may or may not be the trouble with it; I am not giving an opinion on that. This bill, however, is not one for creating employment, as I see it; nor does it deal with questions which create employment. It deals rather with making the act wider in its application, so that persons may be brought within its provisions who do not now come under it. I hope that hon. members will now confine their remarks to the issue.

Mr. Speaker, bowing to your ruling, I would point out to the house
204	HOUSE OF
Unemployment Insurance that a portion of this bill in no way deals with unemployment insurance. In fact it deals with what is called unemployment assistance, which is quite a different thing from unemployment insurance, as was pointed out at the dominion-provincial conference of 1945. Supplementary benefits, under sections 87A and following, are not related to unemployment insurance; they are an alternative to unemployment insurance.
What I was trying to suggest, and I shall not pursue it, was that supplementary benefits, rather than meeting the situation in this country, will merely reach a few who are covered thereby. There will still remain a large area of unemployment about which nothing is being done, either under the Unemployment Insurance Act or under the provision which deals with supplementary benefits.
In 1945 the Minister of Labour made his proposals, and they are of interest today. These were the proposals of the dominion government, and in some parts they are as well forgotten as were those other proposals for social security in connection with old age pensions.
The minister said:
Over the past seven or eight years there have been recommendations by the national employment commission, the Sirois commission and others, that the dominion should assume responsibility for necessary relief to the employable unemployed. It has been generally suggested that the dominion should accept this obligation as part of any general settlement with the provinces.
Then he goes on to say this:
The' dominion government would accept responsibility for ensuring that there shall be provided a reasonable minimum payment for the maintenance of employable unemployed persons through
(a) the extension as rapidly as possible of unemployment insurance to cover all employees.
I point out, sir, that those suggestions were made almost five years ago, and since that time there have been few additions to those who come within the terms of the act. A reference was made today to the inclusion of people who are employed in lumbering and logging. There still remain many other excepted employments which, under the terms of this bill, will not receive anything. Then the Minister of Labour said:
In the period when such extension is being carried out and before insurance benefits properly so-called can be built up, by instituting a system of unemployment assistance to be administered in close co-operation with the unemployment insurance commission.
This is, in fact, what we have here-unemployment assistance. It is called by a different name-supplementary benefits. How far the government has departed from these promises of 1945! With regard to unemployment assistance, which is just another form for the supplementary benefits, the minister said 

that as part of the government's promises to the provinces, in addition to unemployment insurance-I emphasize those words, "in addition to"-the dominion will set up a system of unemployment assistance under which it will pay benefits equal to eighty-five per cent of the unemployment insurance benefits to unemployed persons able and willing to work who are not entitled or have ceased to be entitled to unemployment insurance benefits. Why has that' not been carried out? Why is it now reduced to eighty per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I do not like to rise again, but my hon. friend is continuing to talk about unemployment assistance, which does not involve the principle of insurance. If I sit in my seat and say nothing, in spite of your ruling, sir, I shall be admitting the relevancy of what the hon. gentleman is saying. All this should be said on another occasion. I do not think this is the moment to enter upon a discussion of that problem. We are dealing with an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act, and I submit we should adhere to the ruling.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: On the point of order, I believe Your Honour was correct in the previous ruling to the effect that, in debating this bill, we should debate unemployment insurance and not the methods of providing employment. I believe I am correctly stating what Your Honour ruled. Since that ruling was made, the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has adhered to it. He has not been talking about a means of providing employment; he has been talking about proposed changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act. I say that as long as we stay within that sphere of discussion of the Unemployment Insurance Act, we should be in order.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: If we do that.

Apparently my hon.
friend has not read this.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I have been accused of writing some of it.

I am reading from the dominion-provincial submissions, page 387, a summary of dominion proposals. I can understand my hon. friend's diffidence about hearing a matter such as this discussed, but I am pointing out that it is the same thing as is now brought in under another name, with the exception that the government has not carried out the promise it made in 1945 to provide for eighty-five per cent of the expenditures in connection with these assistance grants.
I submit, sir, that I am in order. If we cannot discuss this matter under unemployment insurance, when the government itself placed

it under that in 1945, then my hon. friend is simply endeavouring to throttle discussion of this matter which is so important to the people as a whole.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext:
From what the minister said I did not gather that he was endeavouring to throttle discussion. He was bringing to my attention the fact that this bill deals with unemployment insurance, and not with benefits which are being paid to people who are unemployed. I gather from the act that this bill deals with persons who have been employed and have been entitled to benefits. Further assistance is being given to them if they previously came within the provisions . of the act. As I said this is quite a long bill. I do not like to be too technical, but I would point out that in dealing with these amendments we are not dealing with the whole Unemployment Insurance Act; we are dealing with certain phases of the act which are being amended.
I would ask hon. members to endeavour to keep their remarks within the confines of the amendments which are now before the house.

Mr. Speaker, may I say a word on the point of order?-because I think we may have to have a decision on it before this matter of debate is finally settled. The only way to understand what we are talking about is to know what the item on the order paper says. Item No. 5 on the order paper reads:
Second reading of Bill No. 8, an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940.
I maintain that the whole Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940, is open for debate. If the minister did not want a full debate he should have taken the precaution to limit the debate by having the title read something like this: "An act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940, extension of benefits." If this had been the title of the bill, we would have been limited to a discussion of extension of benefits; but this is a general revision of the Unemployment Insurance Act, and I am going to have something to say on that when my turn comes. We cannot limit discussion on this bill until we get a new title for it.
Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, second edition, citation 753, reads:
The second reading of a bill is that stage when it is proper to enter into a discussion and propose a motion relative to the principle of the measure.
There is a great variety of principles involved in the measure that is now before us; consequently other amendments can be moved to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Therefore the whole act is now before us.
Unemployment Insurance

May I suggest that this is a bill for insurance against unemployment? If the house is not going to be allowed to discuss unemployment in all its phases, how can it properly be asked to discuss insurance against unemployment? There is no place that I can see in our whole sessional set-up that lends itself more properly to discussion of unemployment, and all the factors that enter into it, than the very bill that we have before us. Surely when we are trying to establish an act for insurance against unemployment, that is the time to discuss unemployment itself. If we cannot do it on this bill, the government might as well say that they are going to close the books on the whole question of unemployment so far as the Commons is concerned. They have closed their eyes up to the present time, and now they are going to close the books.

With great respect, may I point out that I think Your Honour was in error in stating that this bill covered only those employees who have already established entitlement to insurance. That may be true of groups 1 and 2; but if Your Honour will refer to section 20 of the bill you will find in new section 87B that classes 3 and 4 consist of employees who have never had entitlement to insurance. I think that that should make a material difference in the ruling made by Your Honour. It certainly is perfectly obvious that the amendment is not confined to persons who have been entitled to insurance.

I should like to direct the minister's attention to the promise he gave yesterday that he would permit a good deal of latitude if we adopted the resolution. However, sir, some enlightenment may be gathered by looking back at the resolution, which dealt with more than merely special supplementary benefits. The resolution reads:
To provide for supplementary benefits during the winter season in any year and government financial contribution in consequence thereof, for additional insurance coverage, for readjustment and simplification of rates of contribution, and for consequential amendments; to provide also for an increase in the membership of the unemployment insurance advisory committee from six to eight members; and to provide further that the members of the national employment committee shall receive the same remuneration as the members of the unemployment insurance advisory committee.
Bearing in mind the great importance of this subject not only to hon. members but to the hundreds of thousands of people throughout the country, I feel that the minister should now reconsider the suggestion he made to Your Honour and permit the latitude that he promised yesterday.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
For Your Honour's consideration may I also suggest you note that the

Unemployment Insurance amending bill proposes changes in the rates of premium that workers are to pay; it proposes changes in the rates of benefits the workers are to receive; it proposes changes in the statutory conditions under which workers receive those benefits; it proposes changes in the rules of evidence before the courts-
Mr Fournier (Hull): That is not a point of order. The hon. member is making a speech. Why not wait?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
It is a point of order,
because you are questioning whether or not it opens up the whole act. In addition to all these changes, and others that I shall point out in my speech that the Minister of Public Works is talking about, there is a whole new section with regard to supplemental benefits. Actually it is a rewriting of the whole Unemployment Insurance Act. While I stand by my concurrence in Your Honour's ruling that in this debate we have to stick to unemployment insurance, still I submit that Your Honour should recognize that this is practically a whole new Unemployment Insurance Act, and that the whole Unemployment Insurance Act should be up for discussion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext:
I am not entirely in accord
With what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) with regard to this bill permitting a general discussion of the Unemployment Insurance Act. I do not think that merely because a few words are added or omitted in the title of a bill, that would permit or prevent a general discussion. I am inclined to the view that discussion should relate to the principle of the amending bill, irrespective of the title.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) drew my attention to clause 87B. I notice in that clause there is added a class who work in lumbering and logging for at least ninety days in any period of twelve months falling within the year and a half prior to a claim being made. That probably does bring in workers who had never formerly been covered by the act. But they had been employed in a specific industry.
I believe I have made my position clear. The minister did say, and intimated again a moment ago, I gathered, that he does not wish to be too technical. So far as I am concerned, however, I do not think the terms of this bill are wide enough to permit a discussion of the whole question of unemployment. This bill refers, not to methods of providing employment, but to unemployment insurance.

Mr. Speaker, if I understand your direction aright, I am permitted to discuss the question from the point of view
[Mr. Knowles.l
of the 1945 representations made by the government of Canada to the provinces in regard to the question of unemployment insurance, or unemployment assistance.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The first is right, but not to unemployment assistance, unless it is on an insurance basis.
Oh, Mr. Speaker, it was all together in 1945, and it is all together now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: No.

All the government have done is this: they have changed the name from unemployment assistance to supplementary benefits. Your Honour will have noticed how anxious the minister was to raise this, question. Apparently in this way they would endeavour to delude us into believing that they have not departed from the promises they made to the provinces in 1945.
I point out that these were the representations made regarding unemployment insurance and employable unemployed by the Minister of Labour to the premiers and representatives of the different provinces. He made this suggestion:
As rapidly as possible the Unemployment Insurance Act will be widened to embrace all employed persons.
The question necessarily arises now, after five years: Why is it that there are so many excepted classes of persons today who are being passed by in the matter of assistance.
The minister went on to say this:
As already stated the objective would be to bring into insurance in a relatively short time the whole employed population; when this had been accomplished the only employees who might require assistance, ini contrast to insurance, would be those who had exhausted their insurance benefits or failed to qualify.
Those are the same people today who come within the provisions of the supplementary benefits. Then he went on to say:
By that time experience with the extended insurance scheme would enable a decision to be made whether to extend the duration of benefits and shorten the period of qualification for insurance.
The question naturally arises here: Why should not the period of qualification be reduced? Mention has been made of the hundreds of millions of dollars amassed as a result of the contributions. A period of five years has gone by now and experience has shown that the period of qualification should indeed be reduced.
Having pointed out what should be done with those who had exhausted their unemployment insurance benefits, the minister said this:
In the case of an insured person who has exhausted insurance benefits, or who lacks the full qualification for insurance benefits, the scale of

assistance would be approximately eighty-five per cent of the insurance benefit to which such person's contribution class previously entitled him or would in due course entitle him.
I ask the minister this question: Why has there been this change from the eighty-five per cent, the promise made in 1945, to the eighty per cent of today? Why has there been this material change?
In 1945 the Minister of Labour undertook as follows:
Payments for unemployment assistance would be made under authority of an appropriation for this purpose, out of the consolidated revenue fund, and not out of the unemployment insurance fund.
Today the new scheme is this-a complete departure from that of 1945.
Shame.

Today the scheme is that the provision be made for contributions on the part of workers, and in addition to that, in the other provisions, for increasing the ambit of qualifications in the salary limit from $3,120 to $4,800. What the minister is expected to explain to the house and to the provinces-which have no responsibility in connection with unemployables-is why the change that has been made; why the alteration? Who made the recommendation? Did the advisory committee suggest that the promises and pledges of 1945 should be departed from in this manner?
What provision is to be made in connection with supplementary benefits for young men and women who have none of the qualifications to ensure them payment of benefits, and who are unemployed today? What about those in categories not comprised within the act? These are questions which the unemployed in this country expect to have answered.
Instead of saying:	Let us not discuss the
question of unemployment here, surely the minister's attitude should be:	Let us face
it; let us endeavour to arrive at some solution. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) spoke about shutting the book, and about the government shutting their eyes to unemployment. Surely they do not want parliament to shut its mouth on this problem, one which is so important to half a million people in this dominion today.
So far as the general purpose of the bill is concerned, we accept it; but we say it does not go far enough-first, in the matter of the payment of benefits; secondly, in the fact that it is a departure from the promise of 1945, made to the dominion-provincial conference; third, that parliament should consider the period of unemployment for qualification, and its reduction; fourth, that parliament should consider, under this act, the
Unemployvient Insurance inclusion for supplementary benefits of those who today are unemployed and have no one to look to but the federal authority.
The provinces have no responsibility. The Sirois commission report, which I have here, places the responsibility for unemployment expenditures, so far as employables are concerned, on the federal authority; and that responsibility was accepted in 1945. It will not be discharged by an act as incomplete, with its amendments, as is the Unemployment Insurance Act of today.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to associate myself with the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) when, in his opening remarks, he referred to the indisposition of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) and expressed the hope that he may shortly return to the house in his full vigour. I too sincerely hope so. I have been associated with the Minister of Labour for many years and although we have not always seen eye to eye in connection with certain matters I have the highest regard for him.
I spoke yesterday on the resolution stage of this bill and I do not want to repeat anything that I said at that time. If it were not for certain things that have happened I would be quite willing to let this reading go without saying anything at all. But I do protest as strongly as I possibly can against the way the government has treated the house in regard to this measure. We were told-1 shall read the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent)-in so many words that the purpose of this bill was to extend the supplementary benefits and it was desirable that it should go through the house now so that it could be quickly enacted and the benefits paid, despite the fact that on the opening day of this session we passed a resolution providing that the speech from the throne would have precedence over all other business this week and that for next week it would have precedence for three days in the week, with government business having precedence for the other two.
This bill was said to be so important, the purpose it was to fulfil was said to be so important, that we could not wait until next week; it had to be done at once. If the purpose of the bill was what we were told it was last Wednesday I would have no objection. At the adjournment of the house on Wednesday the Prime Minister said, as reported on page 151 of Hansard:
I understand that the Acting Minister of Labour has been discussing with the leaders of the several groups the possibility of taking up tomorrow, notwithstanding the special order made in respect of this debate, resolution No. 10 on today's order paper dealing with unemployment insurance in an effort

Unemployment Insurance to have that resolution considered and the legislation enacted so that the payments it would authorize could be made as from the first of March.
Then the Prime Minister went on to say that he was informed that preparations by the Department of Labour were so far advanced that the benefits would be paid as soon as the legislation was passed, and he continued:
If my understanding is correct, the leaders of the several groups have said that they realize it would relieve distress to have that done as soon as possible.
That was the understanding upon which we allowed this measure to have priority over the debate on the speech from the throne. What have we got? What is placed before us? This is not a short measure to extend the benefits of the act; we have before us a bill of seventeen pages dealing with 25 different sections of the Unemployment Insurance Act. I insist that that is not the way the government should treat this house. This is a general revision of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
When the Unemployment Insurance Act was introduced in 1940 it was referred to a special committee and witnesses from all over the country were heard. We now have a general revision of the act and an attempt is being made to rush it through the house. A great many of those who will be affected by it were not consulted or did not see the bill. As a matter of fact, I did not see the bill until noon today.
We are all in the same position.

A government that wants the co-operation of this house, a government that wants the co-operation of various sections of the community, should not treat this house or the community in that way. I protest the deception that was put over on hon. members of this house.	[DOT]

If the minister thinks that "deception" is a little too strong I am quite willing to have him suggest a more moderate or less extreme or more general word that will meet the situation. In any case I am glad that he admits that there was something put over the house.

After what I have said I find it very difficult, even at Your Honour's request, to withdraw the impression that I have left with the house because that is the impression I got. However, if it is unparliamentary to use the phrase, of course I withdraw it.
Here is the kind of thing that we have in this bill, and this is by no means the most important section in the bill.
Section 87E, dealing with suitable employment, has nothing to do with supplementary benefits. It is not required at all to take care of the critical unemployment situation confronting us today. The section reads:
Any employment that, in the opinion of an insurance officer, a person who claims supplementary benefit is able to perform shall be deemed suitable, notwithstanding paragraphs (b) and (c) of subsection 2, and subsection 3, of section 40 of this act.

That is an important amendment. It varies the principle embodied in the act when it was first drafted. It leaves the question of suitable employment to the insurance officer. I submit to you we should not have amendments of that kind put before us and the house asked to rush them through without giving the people who are affected by the legislation, the people who pay the contributions, an opportunity to see what the effect of the amendments is going to be. I deplore the way this matter has been handled.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a word at this stage. I do not intend to go into the subject of general unemployment although, so far as I know, the government agenda does not provide any other place where we might better discuss that problem. As was expressed clearly the other day by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw), we see no great objection to the amendment in that it gives a little bit more relief to some of those who are unemployed if they come under the legislation. Generally speaking, it seems to me that the bill is not going to benefit a great many more than it did before. It is true that there will now come under the bill some industries which were not included before. The ceiling has been raised from $3,120 to $4,800, and that will bring in a great amount by way of extra contributions. To that extent the fund will be swelled. Whether the increased benefits will be in the same ratio as the increase in collections is problematical. Probably the minister will explain that as we go along. Certainly the benefits that are to be paid under the supplementaries are not going to be sufficient to take care of the problem involved.
One thing that concerns me very much is the thousands of unemployed who are not going to benefit as a direct result of these amendments. When the legislation was introduced I was in hopes that the government would see to it that the amendments to be made to the legislation would be comprehensive enough to cover at least a large majority of the people who are now unemployed. I want to join with the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) in his statement as to the procedure that is being followed in connection with this measure. The amendments presented to us are most complicated when you compare them with the original act, and it seems to me that it will take a tremendous amount of work in order to get the thing in proper shape. In my judgment this is no place to do that. I think it would be far better for the bill to be referred to a committee where it can have the thorough study that it deserves. Otherwise
Unemployment Insurance when the new amendments come into operation we are going to find ourselves in the position where a great many worthy organizations which should have been included under the bill will be exempt. In that respect it is not meeting the conditions for which it is intended. I should think the acting minister would be only too pleased to have the bill referred to a committee. In that way it could be brought back to the house in a satisfactory form to which the whole house could agree. I strongly recommend that procedure to the minister.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join in the protest that has already been made by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). As members in all parts of the house well know, it took the unanimous consent of the house for this measure to be dealt with yesterday and today. I certainly can speak for myself, and I think for others too, when I say that we gave unanimous consent because we were led to believe that the important part, if not the whole of the bill, dealt with ways and means of getting supplementary benefits to certain people now unemployed and not receiving them.
It was pointed out to us that the department had already made the necessary arrangements and that certain cheques, as a matter of fact, could go out right away if we facilitated the passage of the measure. That is the kind of situation that we frequently find ourselves in, but in view of the obvious distress, to use the Prime Minister's word, and the possibility that this measure would provide some relief for that distress we agreed to upset the established procedure for this week and permit the bill to be introduced. On receiving the bill today, an hour or two at the most before the house convened this afternoon, we find it has in it a number of things that call for changes in the basic part of the Unemployment Insurance Act. It is that sort of thing that led my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East, to use language that was regarded as perhaps unparliamentary. But, Mr. Speaker, you can see the situation. I shall not say the same thing, but you can see how we feel. Under the pretext of an emergency we have been given not a simple bill to deal solely with that emergency but a bill that provides pitiable relief of that distress, and along with it makes major and fundamental changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act itself.
The Acting Minister of Labour (Mr. Martin), and the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Labour, who has also had occasion to express this view, know that when we have asked in previous sessions for changes in the

Unemployment Insurance Unemployment Insurance Act-and the same thing happens when we ask for changes in the national labour code-we have been told that this legislation is the result of long consideration. We are told that drafts and subsequent drafts have been referred to the labour congresses, the Canadian Manufacturers Association, and the provincial governments and as a result the legislation that is before the house represents the consensus of the various governmental and other bodies that are interested. Therefore it is said to us that no matter how good the suggestions we offer on the floor of the house it would not be wise to upset legislation that has that kind of support behind it.
This afternoon we receive a bill containing basic and fundamental changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act. I can say categorically that up until three o'clock this afternoon neither the president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada nor the president of the Canadian Congress of Labour had seen a copy of the bill. I do not know whether the employers have seen a copy of it, but I doubt whether they were able to get one either, because it was available only to a few of us when it was first handed around a couple of hours before the house met. That simply is not playing fair with the house, with the people interested in the measure, or with workers across the country or employers either, for that matter. In addition to the statement I made about the top officials of the two labour congresses, I can say that, since reports have appeared in the press as to what is coming, I have had complaints from representatives of labour in this city today as to some of the other changes that are proposed in the measure. My colleague the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) has referred to the amendment having to do with the phrase "suitable employment". Granted that this is tied to the portion of the act which relates to supplementary benefits; still that phrase "suitable employment" has been one of the greatest bones of contention in the Unemployment Insurance Act. We have discussed it and complained about it on the floor of this house time and again, but we have been told it could not be changed without consulting all these people concerned. Now we have an amendment which makes that phrase even worse than it was before, with respect to the payment of supplementary benefits, and we are asked to rush it through.
We find, too, that there has been a change in the statutory condition which requires 180 days' contributions within the last two years. Now we find that in addition an employee seeking benefits must show that he has made at least 60 of those contributions within the last twelve months or 45 within the

last six months. That is not an alternative; it is an addition to the statutory condition which has been there since this act was brought down in 1940. All kinds of workers across this country who have been paying their premiums through the years will feel that in a sense this is the breaking of a contract. True, it is a one-sided contract in that it is legislation which they have to abide by; but these were the conditions under which they have been paying their premiums all this time, and now a change has been made. When I asked officials of the labour congresses here in Ottawa what they thought of this the only answer I could get was, "Well, I have not seen the bill; I don't know what it is all about."

If my hon. friend will permit me, on a point of order I would like to say that everything contained in the present bill which refers to the existing act, changing or clarifying any existing provision, has been submitted to the advisory committee on insurance. This has been stated already, and I should like my hon. friend to take note of it. Part IIA of this bill, having to do with supplementary benefits, did not go to the advisory committee on insurance but went to an interdepartmental committee on social security.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I think you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that this is not a point of order, but I do not mind it as an interjection; as a matter of fact it helps me out. I would point out that in the bill now before us there is an explanatory statement in connection with every clause; and in a number of cases it is stated that the clause in question, either in detail or in substance, has been approved by the national unemployment insurance advisory committee. In some cases, however, that sentence does not appear; and because of the zeal with which that sentence is put in whenever that is the case I can only assume that there are a number of these sections, even in the changes to the original act, about which the advisory committee knew nothing. This conflict between the statement made just now by the parliamentary assistant and the statements made to me by responsible labour leaders strikes me as very strange. They have seen reports of this statement that these matters have been referred to them; yet they say they have not seen them.
I repeat, every time we want to make a change we are told that this legislation has been built up after long consideration and that it cannot be changed without equally long consideration, so it seems hardly fair to bring about these amendments in this unsatisfactory manner. I would point out as well

that changes are proposed in the rates of contributions which employees will make. There are some anomalous details in that connection which I shall not discuss now but will reserve until we get into committee on the bill. It means that once this bill comes into effect many workers across the country are going to find the deduction from their regular pay a little higher than it was before. They are going to wonder what this government and this parliament are doing down here. They think we are doing something to help out the unemployed who need supplementary benefits; but lo and behold, the deduction from their pay cheques is going to be greater. They are going to discover the rather strange fact that the deduction increases by just the same amount for those in the lower categories as for those in the higher ones, with but slight exceptions.
Then there are corresponding changes in the rates of benefits to be paid, all of which are fundamental changes in the basic act itself; yet we are given really no opportunity to pass upon those. There is a little bit.of relief for the distressed in the bill, and if we oppose it or delay it or even have it sent to committee, as was suggested by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston), we will be accused of withholding payments from some of the 70,000 unemployed who might get something under this legislation. There is also a change with respect to temporary unemployment, which seems to be somewhat confused. As a matter of fact a number of the calls I have had today relate to the confusion on that point.
I do think the government does this sort of thing just a little too often. It has something good; it may be little enough, but it is sufficiently good for us to support it. But along with it they include other things that, to say the least, require more mature consideration. So I feel that the protest made by the hon. member for Vancouver East is valid indeed and I support that protest as strongly as I can.

have only a few words to say on this matter at this time. We are dealing now with the principle of the bill, and this is the only chance we will have to say anything in that connection. Well, what is the principle of this bill? As I see it the principle of the bill is to raise more money for the unemployment insurance commission and, as to the benefits to the unemployed that will be paid out for the additional period, to reduce by 20 per cent the payments made by the commission. Stripping this bill of all the legal language, that is exactly what it means to me.
Unemployment Insurance
I am not going to repeat anything that has been said already by the two previous speakers from this group, but I want to emphasize that this is the principle we are dealing with. Throughout the country there is a crisis in employment; and it is growing. In my opinion this bill was designed by t'he government to take the edge off that crisis. We get into a discussion on unemployment, and unless this is understood pretty thoroughly a lot of people are going to assume that this legislation is going to do something about our unemployment problem.
Take this business of increasing the amount of money available to the unemployment insurance commission. The bill suggests a change in connection with employees in the boy class. Previously the employer paid the contribution for that employee. Under the terms of this bill the employee will have to make that contribution himself.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: His own contribution.
That is right; but previously the employer made it for him.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: But he obtained no benefits.

Yes, he did. We can argue that point when we come to the section; I know Mr. Speaker does not want me to go into the bill clause by clause. That change means more money to the commission, with very little increase in benefits. Then you are giving coverage to another income group, up to $4,800 a year, which will include another 90,000 people. In my opinion that is a pretty select group, who are not going to draw on the fund. They are the men in the executive class, and that means more money for the commission. It is throwing the burden for paying for the upkeep of the unemployed on a group of men who, in my opinion, will never receive any benefit from the act. Then, the one cent increase is going to mean a lot of money to the unemployment insurance fund. It would seem, therefore, that the only connection this bill has with the present unemployment' situation is the extension of benefits from January to the end of March and, providing the bill passes this year, until April 15. While the benefits are being extended to people who are unfortunately unemployed for that length of time, the amount payable to them is being cut by 20 per cent. Personally, I cannot justify that principle. So far as I can see, those are the two principles contained in the bill. No. 1 is to get more money for the commission, and No. 2 decreases the rates that are now in existence.
I should like to mention this advisory committee. If you look at the bill, you will find that of all the sections contained in it there

Unemployment Insurance are only two concerning which it is emphasized that the advisory committee has agreed to them in principle. The advisory committee is composed of representatives of labour and of the employers. If these representatives are not going to be consulted when basic changes are made in the act, then the committee serves no useful purpose. The bill provides also for an increase in the number of representatives on the committee. I know the program of labour concerning the changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act. These changes are certainly a long way from it. I am reasonably sure that most of the changes, as the bill itself indicates, were not agreed to by the advisory committee.
In my opinion, that is a serious objection. I know that if I were the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and a man who is as honourable as he is, if I were pinch-hitting for the Minister of Labour, who is unfortunately ill, and I was handed a bill such as this, one of the first questions I would ask the parliamentary assistant would be, "Has this bill been before the employer-employee committee?"

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That was one of the first things I did.
I imagined you would. Then, the parliamentary assistant would have to say, " I am sorry, but only two sections of the bill went before that committee."

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: He said just the opposite.

The bill does not say that. The bill clearly says that the committee agreed upon two matters in principle, one of which was the increasing of the amount of permissible earnings. They are small details. In so far as the basic changes are concerned, such as the rates and the people to be included, I do not think the committee was consulted.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: May I say that on the question of the disappearance of the fraction of a cent in the rate of contribution, the advisory committee was consulted and unanimously agreed the change was reasonable.
I would agree to that myself.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: That is a basic change.

That was not a basic change, that was just a reasonable change. In fact, that was a good change, and I would have agreed to that myself. I do not believe this complicated bookkeeping, and the chasing around of fractions, means anything but a lot of trouble. The committee agreed to that in principle.

As I -said before, the drafters of the bill were careful to write into the bill the few places in which they could say the advisory committee agreed to this in principle. Such was the case in only about one-half of one per cent of the bill. The other changes were not agreed to by that committee. I am deeply concerned about this advisory committee. If it is only to be window-dressing, and to be used merely when the department wants to use it, then I think we should have an understanding on it.
If I were a member of the advisory committee representing labour, and a bill with the far-reaching effect of this bill were brought in by the department, I would certainly disclaim any responsibility and quit the committee. I would have my say or I would not remain on the committee. If the members of this house are assured that neither the employer nor the employee representatives are to be consulted about these things, we can take a different attitude in the house. When I know a committee representing the people vitally concerned in these matters actually functions, I am not so inclined to be suspicious as I would be if the committee were not there. I strongly urge upon the minister and the parliamentary assistant that when matters of this kind are discussed in the future the committee should be used, and thus guarantee that the measure receives some consideration by a committee, which is really the only place such matters can be properly considered.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether I may be allowed to make a few observations at this stage. I am not particularly familiar with the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940, which has had a good many amendments in the past ten years. To be confronted with a bill at three o'clock this afternoon, and to be expected to understand it, would require the wisdom of a Solomon. I know there are a great many wise men here but I do not profess to belong to that class. Because I do not know under what particular section I should bring these points out I should like to be permitted to point out to the minister certain difficulties that have arisen to my knowledge in connection with the administration of this act in Newfoundland.
There is the instance of men who were working on public works and who, prior to the provincial election in May, had to be laid off in accordance with the provisions of the Newfoundland election act of 1913. Before the month had expired some of these had occasion to go and apply for insurance, and they drew six days' insurance. Under the law as it applies to Newfoundland since April 8, 1949, unemployment assistance rather than unemployment insurance was granted, because they had not made any contributions. They went back to work on May 31, and then they were laid off as seasonal workers. The work closed down. When they went to apply for the insurance they were not granted any. They were told that they had received six days' insurance, and that was all they were entitled to until six months had expired. The acting minister, and certainly the parliamentary assistant, knows all about it, and I do not suppose it is anything unusual. It seems to me to be an extraordinary thing that men who have been employed for four years can draw only six days' insurance and were refused any further benefits.
The second class that I wish to bring to the attention of the minister is that of workers on other public works who had to wait five weeks and still have not received their insurance. Acting on their behalf I took up the matter with the local office, and was informed that they were swamped with applications for insurance. But surely, if it is to be of any benefit, it should have been attended to before that length of time had elapsed; otherwise the people had to depend upon charity or they would have starved. Therefore I suggest to the acting minister, and to the minister himself when he comes back, which I hope will be soon,

Unemployment Insurance that some attention should be given to a proper adjudication of those claims. They should not have to wait so long.

On section 3-Rates of contribution.

Mr. Chairman, I should
like to make an observation, if I may, on this section, which has to do with rates of contribution. It may properly be said that because the federal government has gone so far into trade, into business and commerce, in the natural flow of events the question of unemployment and the question of workers' conditions, wages, jobs and so on are predicated to a very great extent upon the policies of the government of the day. At least, when things are good the government takes the credit for it. I suppose when they are bad the government will not be quite so prone to advertise their relationship to that condition, but nevertheless they have to take the bitter with the sweet.
That leads me to this point. The change in the Unemployment Insurance Act, both as to contributions and the other sections as well, is largely brought about by the fact that people have not as many jobs as they did have and that the future of their jobs is much more uncertain than it was a year or so ago. That means that the government has a responsibility with respect to the unemployment situation and the insurance against it. That has been recognized by the fact that the government is now guaranteeing the fund. What it means is that if the fund has not enough money by contributions the government puts up the difference. In establishing that principle with respect to unemployment insurance the government has accepted some responsibility for the matters which are causing the situation which would call for greater benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
The point on which I find myself in great disagreement with the administration is why the government, which has partially accepted responsibility for the condition, asks the worker to put up more money because there is some unemployment which has been caused by policies or conditions which are under the jurisdiction of the government. I think it is adding insult to injury to ask the worker , of this country to underwrite the unemployment situation, even to the degree that the government is now asking him to do so. I do not think the worker should have been asked to do that. In many instances the worker is in a pretty insecure position. I do not think that he should be asked to carry

more of his share with respect to unemployment benefits than he is doing now. It is asking too much of our working people to ask them to increase their contributions in order to relieve unemployment, or the results of unemployment, in the country. So far as this financial measure is concerned, that rests squarely on the doorstep of the government. Surely we are not going to put the unemployment situation over on the doorstep of the workers of Canada, who are themselves likely to feel the pinch as the days go on. That is the thing the government ought to be shouldering. Having accepted that principle, surely there is no reason why they should not have gone that far. There may be valid reasons which dictated the government's position on that. But the government will never get the worker to see that they are valid reasons- and, frankly, I have not been able to see them, either.
I suggest that at this stage the government should consider very carefully whether it should not either change or withdraw the amendment it is making which would have the effect of directing the workers in this country to put up more money for the unemployment insurance fund. It ought to be the other way round. We ought not to be shouldering the worker with more burden; we ought to be taking something off his back, rather than putting it on.
For that reason I suggest that the government ought to retrace its steps and retreat from its position. This amendment is feeble and futile enough as it stands. It is a half loaf being accepted by parliament, rather than nothing. Nevertheless it seems to me we have reached the limit of absurdity when we ask the workers of this country to put up more money to solve the unemployment situation. That is the government's job, not the workers'.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say something similar to what has been said by the hon. member for Peel. I feel that the government, through the acting minister or the parliamentary assistant, must give a full explanation of the basis upon which these new rates were arrived at.
I presume it will be said that in return for the increased amount each worker is being asked to pay he will receive the guarantee of a slightly higher rate of benefit, if he has to go on unemployment insurance. That is an argument which seems to have some logic in it. But it is pretty hard to sell it to the worker who is not anticipating unemployment, but who sees this increase in the amount he has to pay brought in just at a

time when apparently the government is being generous and doing something for the unemployed.
This will look to the workers of this country exactly as it has been described by the hon. member for Peel. It will seem as though the workers are to be asked to pay an additional tax which is said to be necessary to enable the government to send out these cheques-which will go out if and when the legislation passes.
The minister made the statement that the increase was to be one cent a day. Well, that is pretty easy to recite; it sounds very small- just a cent a day. But it happens to be six cents a week by way of an additional deduction from the average worker's take-home pay. I have one or two observations to make in that connection. The first is that, except for some differences which I shall point out later, that six cents is across the board. A person who is making $10 a week and is now paying 18 cents unemployment insurance will pay six cents more. A person who is making $35 a week and is now paying 42 cents a week unemployment insurance will pay six cents more. That is not a very fair method of taxation-to add the full six cents on to the unemployment insurance deductions of the people in those two different categories.
Let us take the case of the boy to whom reference was made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, the boy working for $5.40 a week or less than that. I hope there are not any of them from whom unemployment premiums will be taken. That is a ridiculous wage even for a boy to be receiving. But the provision is here. Under the act as it stood before, a boy making less than $5.40 a week paid no premium out of that amount.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: And received no benefits.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Just a moment; you said that before. He paid no premiums, and had no deductions from his $5.40. The total premium paid for him was 18 cents, 9 cents of which was paid by the employer under the employer's name, and 9 cents paid by the employer on behalf of the boy.
Let us get it straight. A boy who was making $5.40 a week paid nothing out of his own earnings.
Or a girl.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Yes. Anyone making $5.40 a week paid nothing. Under the new provision brought in today such a person will pay 18 cents a week. I have already indicated the gross unfairness of it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
May I give an immediate reply?
