speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Speaking first of the first class in the old scale, the insured earning $5.40, under the age of sixteen, may I say the aggregate number in that category is one-half of one per cent of the total number of insured under the act.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I was going to come to that. I was about to say that if it were only one bo}' in the whole of Canada who, thus far, had been paying nothing into the unemployment insurance fund, but who is now called upon to pay 18 cents a week to help the government hand out these supplementary benefits, then that is a shame and something of which this parliament should not approve.
The parliamentary assistant says that it is less than one-half of one per cent. I would assume therefore that it is more than one boy, or that it is a number of boys-perhaps one or two hundred. Offhand I do not know what the number is; but I submit it is bad enough to assess an extra six cents against the person making $10 a week equally as against the person making $35. And certainly it is adding insult to injury to pick out the boy who makes only $5.40 a week, and to ask him to pay 18 cents-
This is insurance; this is not assistance or relief.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I know it is insurance; and the parliamentary assistant is now underlining our complaint about the whole bill, namely that under the pretext of an emergency, or the pretext of an extreme urgency to deal with distress, the government has brought in basic changes in the act. I believe changes should be made in the act, and I have argued for those changes ever since I came here. But the time to deal with them is when we have sufficient time to go into them on a proper basis, instead of going at it with a gun at our heads, as at the present time.
I have gone out, as has the hon. member for Vancouver East, and pointed out to working people that this is insurance. That is what labour asked for, and it is a good thing to have. But it is a strange coincidence to have to provide these increases in amounts just at a time when the government is apparently being generous and giving supplementary benefits to some of the thousands now drawing nothing at all.
I submit there is a coincidence here which will be pretty hard for the government to explain. However, I want them to do it. I want them to explain how they arrived at this new scale, and why it is six cents across the board. It is not completely so, because I realize there are one or two places where

Unemployment Insurance there is no increase because of an overlapping of the old group with the new; and there are one or two places where the increase is only three cents, and one place where it is nine cents. Also, for those in the highest brackets the increase will be twelve cents a week. I would point out at the same time that the increases on the part of employers are not quite the same. Because of this equalization of payments between employers and employees the extra amount to be paid by employers is not as great as the extra amount to be paid by employees.
There has to be some explanation of this- not just figures drawn out of a hat. I think the question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Lake Centre should be answered now and we should be told how much the government expects to get because of these increased rates. Again quoting the hon. member for Lake Centre, I think when we get to the supplementary benefits section we should be given figures showing how much the government expects it will have to pay out. It looks as though these rates are being increased under the pretext of their being insurance when in fact they simply represent the money necessary to pay out these supplementary benefits.

I should like to say a word about the levies that are provided by this section. I pointed out this afternoon that at the dominion-provincial conference of 1945 representations were made by the dominion government through the Minister of Labour as follows, and I quote from page 387 of the proceedings:
In addition to unemployment insurance, the dominion will set up a system of unemployment assistance under which it will pay benefits equal to eighty-five per cent of unemployment insurance benefits, to unemployed persons able and willing to work who are not entitled, or -who have ceased to be entitled, to unemployment insurance benefits. This assistance will be limited to two years of continuous assistance, but a person will again become eligible for this assistance following an approved period of employment.
As I pointed out this afternoon, unemployment assistance is just another way of saying supplementary benefits, the phrase used in this bill. I feel that the charging and imposition of these levies on the employer and employee are a denial of. the representations made to the provinces in 1945 by the Minister of Labour. It is inexcusable and should not be done. In 1945 the Minister of Labour undertook on behalf of the dominion government to provide all of this unemployment assistance.
What is the justification for this further levy? It is a denial of what was promised in 1945. It is all very well to say it is a small levy, but the dominion government undertook at the conference in 1945 to provide


unemployment assistance for the persons covered by this bill under the heading of supplementary benefits. Has consideration been given to this by the provinces? Have they been consulted? This is in fact a travesty of what was undertaken in 1945 at the dominion-provincial conference.
Not only do I disagree with the amount of the levy, I disagree with the right to impose the levy in view of what the Minister of Labour said in 1945. I ask the minister: Is not the provision of these benefits the same thing that the Minister of Labour undertook in 1945 would be supplied by the dominion government at the expense of the people of Canada as a whole?
That is what was promised. You can change the name and call them supplementary benefits instead of unemployment assistance as it was called in 1945; it is the same thing. I submit that it is unjustifiable that a further levy should be made in order to meet this so-called extraordinary situation, incidental as the government claims, to peculiarly difficult climatic or local transitory conditions that will soon pass away. That is the government's allegation, it is not ours.
That being so, what justification is there to impose a levy on the man who works to meet a situation that the government says is transitory, to provide for supplementary benefits? As a matter of fact, this whole question of supplementary benefits is being dragged in by the back door into the Unemployment Insurance Act. There is no justification whatsoever for that. There is no unemployment insurance act that I know of that provides for supplementary benefits such as are being provided for here, and I have read the United States and the British acts. This looks like another scheme whereby the responsibility of the dominion government as enunciated by the Minister of Labour in 1945 is being evaded through the subterfuge of changing names.
I protest most strongly against a further levy being made against the man who works to provide for a situation which the government says is transitory and local, which is the result of conditions peculiar to various areas, rather than having this considered as a national unemployment situation. This is the type of expenditure that the government has always had to make since 1945. Prior to 1945, as is shown in the debates from 1928 to 1945, there was an endeavour to place upon the provinces or the municipalities responsibility for those in this category. In 1945 the government accepted the sole responsibility of providing for unemployment in the transitory sense.

It is not a large contribution that is being asked for, but the principle is wrong and unjust. However small it may be, when a principle is at stake there is good reason to object to a levy such as is being made here.

I think before we pass this section we should be clear in our minds as to just what is involved. During my speech yesterday the Acting Minister of Labour informed us most emphatically that the purpose of this amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act was not to provide a substitute for employment, that it was not a measure to take care of unemployment, that it was simply a redrafting of the act.
We are told in the explanatory note opposite page six that the purpose of the additional cent per day is to provide part of the money that will be paid out in supplementary benefits and that supplementary benefits are being provided because of the unemployment situation during certain months of the year. Regardless of what the minister has said, this is the government's method of meeting the unemployment situation during these particular months.
Working people are being called upon to contribute from their earnings in order to provide money that the government will pay to the unemployed during certain seasons of the year. The government has completely reversed its policy in regard to providing for unemployment. As yet we have had no indication that the government has any other measure to bring before this house to take care of the unemployment situation. I am quite sure that the workers will resent the government calling upon them tq finance an unemployment situation in this country which has always been the responsibility of the federal government.
There is one question I should like to ask. I note that the inclusion of a .new class is recommended by the unemployment insurance advisory committee. Did the unemployment insurance advisory committee also recommend the increases that are in this table? I think we should have a direct answer to that question.

Before the minister answers, I should like to add my voice to those who have said already that it is not just or sound to expect workers across Canada to have to make contributions on this increased scale, which will be permanent contributions, made a part of the act, in order to provide, as the explanatory note makes clear, for the supplementary benefits outlined in clause 20. In other words, for the sake of getting benefits for three months in the year under a situation which, as the hon. member for Lake Centre so
Unemployment Insurance clearly pointed out, the government itself says is only transitory and results only from extraordinary winter conditions, they are going to increase the contribution by six cents per worker forever or for however long he may work. That is exactly what is being done. It is not justified by the situation. It is contrary to the promises which were made, that the dominion government would assume full responsibility for this. No necessity for it has been demonstrated in the course of the remarks of the minister. I certainly suggest the committee should not pass the section until that necessity is proved, and I personally do not believe it can be proved. Before we go any further I think we should have an answer from the minister as to how much these increased contributions are expected to yield, and how much it is anticipated that the increased benefits for these three months of the year will cost.

It appears to me that the hon. member for York South and the hon. member for Kamloops are taking the stand that workers will be opposed to this increase. If I were looking at it from a selfish point of view, representing merchants and retailers, I could take the same stand, but I am not. Organized labour advocated a measure of this kind for years and' they were pleased at the time unemployment insurance was brought into effect because it was insuring their future in the same way that we as individuals insure our lives or make provision for our own protection and that of our families by investments, pension schemes, or annuities. I think you get out of this world what you put into it, and if we are going to ask for greater protection and the extension of the benefits, then it is only natural that we must pay. At the time when the measure was first introduced we enjoyed an exceptionally high state of employment and prosperous times, and I think it was most opportune that it should have been introduced then. Employment has increased since then.
I have particularly in mind the last class, $48 a week or more. That should bring in a large amount, and while I, like other members, am concerned about the actual return in dollars and cents from the one cent addition in the various other classes, I am wondering what amount the category to which I have referred will bring in. Is the minister prepared to tell us the amount expected from that particular class?
I feel that workers as a whole, as well as merchants, realize that these increases must come from one source only. After all, the government makes a 20 per cent contribution to the general fund just as other contributions are made. The more you dip into the fund

Unemployment Insurance "the more you are going to take from the productive pool created by the efforts of the workers and those who are interested in enterprise. For that reason I am inclined to differ from members who have taken the opposite view, and I welcome the measure if there is going to be greater security so far as the insurance angle of the act is concerned.

I do not think that those members who have criticized these particular amendments have done so so much because of the increase in the contribution as they have because of the fact that the amendments have been introduced without consultation with representatives of those who are to make the contributions. That is one basis on which we object to it. Before unemployment insurance was provided for on the statutes, organized labour had advocated it Tor many years. Hon. members of the house will recall when unemployment insurance was eventually put on the statutes. It was not done because the government believed in unemployment insurance but because they wanted to use the contributions to unemployment insurance to prevent the development of the inflationary trend at that time. The two matters coincided, and perhaps it is just as well that they did or we would never have got unemployment insurance.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I have listened with a great deal of interest to what has been said. I have no hesitation in saying at once-and I know something about labour in this country-that I am sure every worker in Canada will be willing to pay six cents a week, as a result of this unemployment insurance amendment, in order to assist, under a pattern of supplementary insurance system, in giving him benefits during the winter months if during that period he finds himself out of work. I have no doubt about this and anyone who does not share that view has not the confidence in Canadian labour that I have. What are we doing in this measure? We are extending the principle of unemployment insurance by way of three partners, the employer, the worker and the state. That is the principle which makes the Unemployment Insurance Act the sound measure that it is.
It would have been possible for the administration to alter its course and, instead of exacting premiums from the beneficiaries, to have paid the whole shot itself. But what
fMr. Isnor.]

does that mean? The government merely represents the taxpayers as a whole, and if the government paid the whole contribution not only would it be betraying the principle of insurance but it would also simply be transferring away from the same quarter moneys that it is collecting now in accordance with insurance principles. I think we are developing in this country, and properly so, the idea that our social services, in so far as they lend themselves to this kind of remedy, should be paid for by contributions from those who are possible beneficiaries. What do we find the situation to be in this house with regard to old age pensions? There is a demand, a desire and an expression of opinion that we should develop pensions on the basis of contributory principles, and in so far as that is practicable I hope, as the Prime Minister has said, that it will be possible to do so.
Could we at this stage, when we have built up a great tradition in the administration of unemployment insurance, betray that principle? I do not think that upon reflection any hon. members, even those who have criticized the bill, will come to that conclusion. As I said last night, and as the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) urged me to say, the unemployment insurance fund must remain intact; it must not lose its trust character. One way to make sure that does not happen is to see that no agency, including the state, is allowed to alter it, directly or indirectly, in such a way as later to lead to impairment of that fund. If my hon. friend will recollect the words of the prime minister of this country in 1935, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, in addressing himself to the measure he introduced, and which was later declared by the courts to be unconstitutional, he will see that Mr. Bennett made this very point, indicating the necessity of providing safeguards with respect to this fund. I do not think one needs to say any more on that point.
In spite of what the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) insists on repeating, even in view of what I said last night, this is not an employment measure. Anyone in his right senses knows that even a government of which my hon. friend has such a low opinion is not so lacking in ordinary intelligence as to make such a declaration of purpose. Of course this is not a measure to relieve unemployment.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Read the speech from the throne.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
This is exactly what it says, a measure intended to provide benefits for those who suffer the condition against which provision is made in this act, by way of

insurance in which they participate, during a period when historically the unemployment rate in our country is higher than in the other months of the year. That is what this measure is, and nothing more. As far as I am concerned, as one member of the government I shall be ready to deal with that other matter when that is to be done, in the way I think it should be dealt with. But let us keep in mind the matter that is engaging us at the present time.
My last comment is in connection with what the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has said twice today. He said it well, but that does not make it a correct or valid argument. He keeps confusing unemployment assistance with assistance made possible by way of an insurance measure. By no possible construction does this come within the ambit of unemployment assistance. The hon. member referred to the discussions of 1945. Of course proposals were made at that time by this government, and in their broad objectives those proposals are still in mind and have not been abandoned.
And have not been kept.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Undoubtedly they will be discussed when the provinces meet next September, and we will have to face such issues. The matter now before us has nothing to do with that kind of assistance. This is not assistance; it is insurance, to which the state and the two partners in industry, the employers and the employees, are contributing. It is a wise principle, which is not new to unemployment insurance. The only criticism that in the circumstances could be legitimately made, I think, is that instead of thinking about this measure today it might have been thought about in 1940 when the original act was introduced. But of course hindsight is always better and more brilliant than foresight. So I say that instead of in any way weakening this principle of contribution, we on this side believe in it, and we feel that the workers of Canada will subscribe to that belief.

I want to say just a few words with respect to the actual insurance. I heartily endorse this measure, and I think we should put it through as quickly as possible so the boys who need this money will get their cheques on March 1. As I see it, however, one thing is left out that I should like to see put in. Take the man who comes out of the mine, the man who comes off the railroad, who goes to a doctor and suddenly finds that he has cancer, or something else radically wrong that cannot be helped. He is out of a job; and he is out of unemployment insurance. That man has paid his
Unemployment Insurance insurance, and he is going to pay more now; and I believe that man should be taken care of.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I want to respond to the challenge of the minister. I do not think this is any sort of lesson to be giving the boys and girls of this country in social responsibility, to put this sort of thing on their shoulders now.
Let me go further. Do not forget that when I first got to my feet I stressed the fact that we want to know what these new rates are going to produce, and I want to know that before this section passes. The senior member for Halifax said a moment ago that employees would be glad to pay these increased rates, because of the increased insurance they were getting for them. I believe he said that, as an employer, he was willing to pay these increased rates too. He has in mind, of course, the statement of the Acting Minister of Labour concerning the one cent per day or six cents per week across the board for employees and employers alike. May I tell the senior member for Halifax and others that in the case of all those earning less than $15 per week, there is to be no increase in the amount paid by the employer. Just let that sink in for a moment.
Let ys take the table that is on page 2 of the bill before you, and compare it with the

old schedule which appears on page 43 of the latest office consolidation of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Here are the facts. In the case of those who were previously making less than $5.40 per week, the employer has been paying a total of 18 cents. He will still pay the 18 cents, so there will be no increase for the employer, but there is an 18 cent increase for the employee. In the case of those earning between $5.40 and $7.49 per week, formerly the employer paid 18 cents. He will still pay 18 cents, so there is no increase. The employee was paying 12 cents and he will now pay 18 cents; an increase of 6 cents. The next group covers those earning from $7.50 to $8.99. The employer was formerly paying 24 cents per week and he will now pay only 18 cents a week; a drop of 6 cents. In the case of the employee, the payment goes up from 15 cents to 18 cents; an increase of 3 cents. The next group is from $9 to $9.59. Formerly the employer was paying 24 cents, and he still pays 24 cents, so there is no increase. The employee was paying 15 cents and now pays 24 cents, an increase of 9 cents. The next category covers those earning $9.60 to $11.99. The employer was paying 24 cents and still pays 24 cents, no increase. The employee was paying 18 cents and is now paying 24 cents, an increase of 6 cents. The next group is from $12 to $14.99. The employer was contributing 24 cents and still contributes 24 cents, no change. The employee was contributing 21 cents, and will now contribute 24 cents, an increase of 3 cents.
The dividing lines with respect to those categories have been changed, so I have had to break them into different groups so as to make the calculations accurate. I have taken all cases up to $14.99 per week, and have shown you that in no case is the employer paying any more, and in one small section the employer is actually paying 6 cents less. In all cases, the employees are paying more, varying from 3 cents to 6 cents and 9 cents and, in the case of those 15,000 boys and girls 18 cents, to provide $125,000 for the fund. To talk about high-sounding principles with these features of this bill is a distortion of those high-sounding principles. Certainly the members of this house support the insurance principle, and support the value of the people of the country knowing that they are paying for what they are getting. It is a distortion of that principle, however, to ask those people in these lower brackets to pay these additional amounts. I protest against it most strongly.
Unemployment Insurance I still say we should have some explanation as to how this scale of rates was arrived at. We should be told, and I hope the members will continue to support me in that, what the governments expects these new rates to provide by way of actual increase in revenue to the fund.

I think that this is the root of the whole bill, and that we should have more information. When this act was first passed it came before the house for analysis, and went to a committee. After much work in committee it came back to the house.
In changing the basis of contribution the minister has asked us to vote on that change with practically no information as to how he arrives at the figures he has given us. In my opinion this is not insurance any more; it is an indirect levy. It is taxation.
The minister also states that the advisory committee had looked at this and approved. The act does not indicate that; but there is a section in the bill which definitely sets out that the committee were consulted. So far as I am concerned, the meagre amount of benefit in this for those who are affected byprolonged unemployment is overshadowed by this inequality in the matter of imposing the rates on the lower income groups. As one member who would like to see this bill go through for the benefit of the unemployed, for whatever benefit there may be in it, I am prepared to say that it should stand and go before a committee for a thorough analysis. I say that because the government is attempting to go right to the roots of the whole Unemployment Insurance Act.
Every time I listen to a discussion of this kind in the house it indicates one thing to me, and that is the necessity of the government getting down to the business of writing an over-all social security act for the people of this country, which would embrace all these things on a contributory basis. With the overlapping of administration costs, and all that kind of thing, this is far from satisfactory. I know it is far from what organized labour in this country is asking. If we close-this act now and accept the contributions on the basis the minister is proposing to us, it may be a long time before the act is reopened.
I would suggest seriously to the minister that this be done. If he wishes to go through the rest of the bill he will find it is only incidental. This section is the basis of the whole thing, and we should have a better understanding of it before it passes.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has criticized the point of view as expressed by me on behalf of the contributing employer group. The hon. member for Cape Breton South states that this is a.

Unemployment Insurance direct tax. If he is correct, then the direct tax, in so far as the benefit is concerned, applies only to the employer group because they pay 40 per cent of the total amount without receiving any direct benefit.
In other words, they pay 50 per cent of the amount contributed, to make up the weekly payments by employer and employee. They receive no benefit directly or indirectly from that payment. The government pays the other 20 per cent. That is why I say the employer is paying 40 per cent of the total amount toward an insurance plan which is entirely for the benefit of the employee.
I believe I should put this on record to offset the argument advanced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre respecting the low scale of the smaller group in this scheme. I wonder if he realizes just what type of employee that includes. In the great majority of cases it would be a parttime employee or a boy or girl working after hours. Perhaps they may receive a small amount for working after school hours. Perhaps that is another point which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has overlooked.
After all, there are only three types of insurance in which we are interested. First there is the type which we pay ourselves by way of individual insurance. These are amounts which we lay aside either in the form of investment, life insurance, annuities or some other forms of insurance from which we benefit. In that connection we pay the direct cost.
The second type is group insurance in which both employer and employee participate. The third is the one we are now considering, which comes under the Unemployment Insurance Act, where the employer, the employee and the government each pay a proportion. As stated before, the employer pays 40 per cent, the employee pays 40 per cent and the government pays 20 per cent, which makes up the total cost of the payments. Through the years the employer pays without receiving any personal benefit.
I submit that the group represented by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Cape Breton South are unfair to the very people they pretend to represent, labour, or at least that is what they tell us. In 1940 and previous years organized labour was in favour of a system of unemployment insurance such as we now have. As far as I know they were 100 per cent in favour of this act. The objections being raised to bringing these amendments into effect come from the group which pretends to represent labour. For the life of me I can-


not follow their argument. This should be placed on the record so that the workingman throughout the country will know the position taken by the C.C.F. on this occasion.

It will need only a short answer to reply to the argument put forward by the senior member for Halifax. The hon. member is correct when he says that organized labour was in favour of the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1940, but this bill is changing that act in regard to a special class of contributors. No evidence has been brought before this committee to show that organized labour either has been advised of the changes or has indicated approval. Unless the senior member for Halifax can bring forward that evidence his argument is so much eyewash.
To answer the hon. member may I say that the employee representative on the advisory committee has seen these amendments and the advisory committee has informed the government-
We have no evidence that this bill was ever before the advisory committee, or that the committee have approved of it.

The argument just advanced by the senior member for Halifax is really not an argument; it was just wishful thinking. He hopes that someone will read that statement in Hansard and fall for it. A great percentage of the people in this country are a little better informed on that subject than he thinks they are.
That is why they do not take very much stock in what the hon. member says.

If it were not for men like myself there never would have been an Unemployment Insurance Act. I can recall sending resolutions thirty years ago to Liberal and Tory governments in this country asking for an unemployment insurance act. That practice was followed through the years. I was a member of this house when this act was brought down and we welcomed it because we realized that this was the fulfilment oi 25 years of effort. We finally convinced those in authority that such an act was a good thing to have.
I remember the opposition there was to this act when this House of Commons was lobbied by representatives of the manufacturers association and other agencies which were opposed to the interests of the working people. They have opposed it right through and they still oppose it. Fortunately for the government and for this act there was a war on which looked as though it might last a little while. It was thought to be a good

time to gather a fund against the anticipated depression that would take place after the war.
I have no illusion as to how the workingman feels about this act, but I do not want to get into an argument on that because I am more concerned about this particular measure. I do not want to see the efforts of thirty years chiselled away, perhaps unconsciously, by people who are advocating this bill at this time. I would rather have the old act without this bill.
The senior member for Halifax says that industry contributes 40 per cent toward the maintenance of the unemployed and gets no benefits. He would seem to indicate that they just throw in 40 per cent out of the goodness of their hearts. But at the end of the year when the employer is reckoning his income tax, the total amount paid to the unemployment insurance fund is written off. In the final analysis the taxpayers of the country are making his contribution. If industry did not have an unemployment insurance fund at this time which had been contributed to on a three-way basis they would be paying heavy taxes for the purpose of taking care of the totally unemployed. I just would not want to see this country with the unemployed that we have without this measure to cushion it. It is a good thing for all concerned that the act is there.
There are two main objections that I have. First, the fund was set up on an actuarial basis. The minister is not able to tell us how they arrived at the figures and the chances are that they may upset the actuarial apple cart. We do not want to see that happen. Let us have it understood that the hon. member for Halifax is an employer. He tells us that labour is in favour of this, when the fact is that labour has never seen it. I hope the minister will give us a pretty full explanation of what is happening to section 28 of the original act by virtue of this amendment. Among the classes of persons to whom these regulations apply are persons employed in the shipping industry, or transportation by water as it is described in the act. At first employment in the shipping industry was not considered as an insurable risk or hazard under the act, but I believe it was two years ago that this principle was abandoned by the commission and the act was amended to bring the industry within its scope at the particular request, I am told, of the seamen of the great lakes. The industry was, however, brought under the act under certain restrictions or special conditions. These special conditions are set out at pages 44 and 45 of the regulations and special orders of the unemployment insurance commission made under section 38 of the act. Subparagraph 5 (b) of section 12 of "Seasonal regulations" reads as follows:
"Seasonal industry" means and includes the following respective industries, which the commission hereby declares to be seasonal industries:
(i) the industry of transportation by water on any of the "inland waters of Canada" as the latter expression is defined in the Canada Shipping Act, 1934, herein referred to as "transportation by water":

(ii) the industry of stevedoring in any of the inland or deep sea ports, herein referred to as "stevedoring."
Subparagraph (c) goes further and says:
(c)	"inland port" means a port on any of the said inland waters of Canada.
In subparagraph (d) deep sea port is described as follows:
(d)	"deep sea port" means the port of Halifax, Nova Scotia and the port of Saint John, New Brunswick.
In subparagraph 4 of the same section 12 of the regulations made under section 38 of the act it is further said:
(4) The off-season applicable in the case of any such seasonal worker shall be determined in accordance with the following rules:
(a) where the particular seasonal industry applicable in his case is transportation by water, the offseason applicable shall be the off-season for transportation by water, namely, the period commencing on December 16 in each year and ending on April 14 next thereafter.

If I may assist my hon. friend, I suggest that he is not reading from the latest regulations of the commission. These were tabled just a few days ago, and they are dated at the end of last December. The regulations provide that the line of division between deep sea and inland waters is Cap des Rosiers. To relieve the mind of my hon. friend I suggest that this is a matter which might be placed before the commission, which has power under the act to give consideration to any representations of this kind and to submit proposals to the governor in council if special regulations should be found desirable.

To deal with the first point raised by the parliamentary assistant, I was quoting from the office consolidation dated October, 1948, which last night he suggested I should get from the library. In any event, I have not yet quoted anything having to do with home trade and inland waters.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: To make the position clear, as far as the act is concerned the consolidation of October, 1948, is the latest; but the latest copy of the regulations dates back to December, 1949, only.

Nothing I have quoted, I am sure, has been amended in the latest edition of the regulations to which the parliamentary assistant refers. I refrained from speaking on the resolution or on second reading because I did not want to delay this important bill. I shall be very brief, but I make these remarks at this point because I do not quite agree with the parliamentary assistant when he says that what I suggest should be corrected with respect to this particular industry can be done only by

Unemployment Insurance order in council or by regulations. I am not sure of that; and I do not know how the parliamentary assistant can be sure of it, because I have not yet fully stated my case. If I may be permitted I should like to proceed, and I shall be as brief as possible.
I was saying that we had created a special category for those employed in the inland shipping industry. If during this off-season period from December 16 to April 14 an employee loses his employment, he has to prove 420 contributions instead of the 180 which are asked of those in other categories.
I am not sure of this, and I have been unable to check it, but I am told that recently this number of 420 was reduced somewhat but that it is still very much higher than the minimum of 180 days required in other categories.
Now I come to the other remarks of the parliamentary assistant. The inland waters of Canada were defined in the Canada Shipping Act as, at their eastern limit, commencing at a line drawn from Father Point to Point Orient on the north shore of the St. Lawrence. As everyone knows, a year ago this limit was changed and put some three hundred miles further down the river, so that it is now a line drawn from Cap des Rosiers through the western point of Anticosti island to the north shore. That required no change in the regulations, because the regulations accepted the description of inland waters contained in the Canada Shipping Act, and when the Canada Shipping Act was changed this definition was automatically changed in the regulations.
Now I come to my second point. I want to make it clear that my remarks apply to seamen no matter where they come from, as long as they are engaged in the specified trades to which I am going to refer. But while my remarks apply to all those seamen they are made particularly in reference to seamen belonging to my own province. In Quebec we have ships sailing from the inland ports of Montreal and Quebec but going further down than the eastern limit of our inland waters. They go as far as Gaspe, the Magdalen islands, Newfoundland, New Brunswick and Labrador. Quite wrongly, I am convinced, these have been classified as inland water ships. They are not; they are in the home trade. Their officers must have the certificates of competency required for the home trade of Canada. More than that, the men employed on those ships can very easily, as they have been doing for a number of years, find employment during the off season on the St. Lawrence on ships sailing from Halifax or Saint John or Sydney, and even on ships which during the summer months are engaged in the St. Lawrence trade but in the winter
236	HOUSE OF
Unemployment Insurance months go to the gulf of Mexico and carry on their trade there. So I say that the risk of unemployment for the men employed in our home trade is not the same as that for those employed in our inland water trade, meaning by that term our great lakes seamen, for instance.
I point out that this situation has created severe hardships in many cases. I feel that, if under this section the commission is to be empowered to make regulations concerning inland shipping, it should be made clear that those regulations are not to extend as they have in the past-unjustly, I say-to seamen engaged in the home trade rather than the inland trade of Canada. That is why I consider it my duty to make these remarks at this stage, when we are discussing the very section which empowers the commission to do the things I am complaining about. I know it might be possible to remedy the situation 1 have outlined simply by amending the regulations, but I contend that if the commission had not such indefinite power it would not be tempted to pass regulations which would affect our home trade, as it has done in the past.
I have another suggestion to put forward in this connection. When we say that the seamen employed on ships sailing in the inland waters of Canada are employed in a seasonal occupation, and should therefore be asked to comply with severe conditions in order to secure benefits under the act, we are not being fair to these men. We should allow them, before they apply for benefits, to declare themselves available for employment in similar industries, or for employment which can be found for them in other industries.
In order to clarify what I mean, may I cite the example of a cook on a ship. A cook on a ship can be just as good a cook in a lumber camp during the winter months, or any other industry in which a cook is required. Another example is a deckhand on a ship. He is used to doing all sorts of work on the ship, such as handling the cargo and various other deck jobs. Such a man could do similar work in other industries in which employment can be found the year round. The case of motor mechanics is similar to that of men working in other industries whether they are handling gasoline or steam engines. These motor mechanics may be employed on a ship on the great lakes during the summer for example, but that does not prevent them from finding employment in a garage in Windsor, for instance, during the winter, or in any other industry in which motor mechanics are needed. I do not think these men should be deprived of their benefits through

the severe restrictive conditions imposed by the regulations, just because they happen to work for five or six months a year in what we call the shipping industry.
The other day I asked an official of the unemployment insurance commission of my province what happened to the employees of summer hotels, such as those which exist in my province. Some of these hotels are operated by the Canada Steamship Lines at Tadoussac and Murray Bay and operate from May or June until September only. Their employees are seasonal employees but because they can find employment in other hotels in other parts of the province or Canada during the winter months they are considered as a regular insurable class. I asked this official why the same thing was not done for the cook, motor mechanic or deckhand on our ships and he had no answer to explain the severe treatment of our seamen.
On many occasions in this house, the senior member for Halifax has mentioned the case of stevedores in connection with unemployment insurance benefits. Recently, I had occasion to join with him in making representations to officials of the government requesting that something be done for them. Surely, those men are eligible for employment during their off-season period in other industries where men are needed to handle heavy cargoes or to perform other work for which stevedores are trained.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, I thought it my duty to make these remarks because I believe it is an important subject. With the decline in our shipping activities, our seamen are finding it difficult to secure employment. I am in favour of the loggers, and the men employed in the lumbering industry in general getting their share of benefits, but I believe our seamen are entitled to the same treatment, because their trade is being severely hit today. I hope these remarks will be taken in good part by the parliamentary assistant, and the minister, as well as the officials of the commission. I hope prompt action will be taken in this respect.

I have been waiting for this clause to be called, because there is a question or two I should like to ask about it. I do not know whether this clause governs those classes that are known as excepted or exempted classes, but I should like to know if the commission has the power to determine what classes shall come under the act and what classes shall be exempted from it. When I refer to classes, I mean people such as I referred to yesterday, hospital employees. They do not come under the act. My question does not concern hospital employees, and

1 only use that as an illustration. My question is, does the commission have power to include or exclude those particular people?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The commission has power, under section 86 (2), to do that very thing. I recall that, because I was reading it last night. Of course, the recommendation of the commission is subject to the approval of the governor in council.

What is the government's reaction to the suggestion that those classes be written into the act instead of being included by order in council, or upon the recommendation of the commission? I believe the act should be changed every time that is done. I refer to classes of people that might number in the thousands. What I have in mind, Mr. Chairman, is this, and you will appreciate the significance and importance of it:	When by regulation, whether it is by
order in council or whatever it may be, certain classes of people are compelled to contribute to a scheme of this kind, then we are imposing a form of taxation. Some other terminology can be used if one desires, but that is what it is. In principle, therefore, you have a small commission authorized-we shall at least give them this benefit-to recommend to the government, and then the government, by order in council, takes the authority of imposing what I am going to call taxation. So far as I am concerned, that is what it is.
Now, I do riot agree with that principle. I believe that action of that sort should be taken by parliament. It is for that purpose the members are here. I should like to know what the government's answer is to the question of why these classes cannot be set out in the act, and the act changed from time to time as required.

I was about to raise the same question as that raised by the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat. My question was in connection with hospitals, which are charitable institutions, and are exempt under the act. I know that hospitals and charitable institutions are exempt under the act. I understand that by order in council or otherwise there is likely to be something, perhaps under the provision of this very section that we are dealing with, so far as seasonal employment is concerned. On two occasions I was given the assurance by the minister, in answering questions put to him by hon. members, that hospitals and charitable institutions were not to come within the purview of this act. Something is said about seasonal employment. I have no doubt that the commission has the power to include seasonal employees who are employed by hospitals and charitable institutions. I only want to say that it will be a real hardship. I do not exactly know how they are going to collect from hospitals on account of seasonal employees. I see some difficulty about that; but even if they had no difficulty about it I am objecting right now to the commission passing any such regulation. My objection may fall on deaf ears because they have the power to do it. But I am objecting on behalf of the hospitals of my province, because there is not one hospital in that province that is making a dollar. They are going into the red every year, and they are supported by the charity of the people. Every year they come around asking for donations from every man, woman and child in the province who has a cent to spare for charitable institutions. It would be a hardship and a wrong to impose upon hospitals down there. I know something about it. I have been chairman of the commission of Victoria General hospital for twelve years. I have connections with some other hospitals in the city of Halifax and also in the constituency I represent. I am only suggesting to the minister tonight that the provisions of this act be not so worked that even seasonal employees of hospitals will come within the purview of the act, thus bringing hospitals within it to a certain extent.

Note this:
-to unemployed persons able and willing to work who are not entitled, or who have ceased to be entitled, to unemployment insurance benefits.

Unemployment Insurance entitled, or have exhausted their entitlement, to unemployment insurance benefits. Then the same paragraph goes on:

So the whole idea that was being put forth at the dominion-provincial conference of 1945 and 1946 under the name of unemployment assistance is precisely that of which we are now getting a partial implementation. There can be no argument about it at all. The idea then was the extension of unemployment insurance, and it was noised from one end of the country to the other that that was one of the things the dominion was prepared to do, namely to recognize its responsibility for the employable unemployed.

In fact this sort of bill underlines the growing need in this country for a piece of legislation that will provide over-all social security. This piecemeal business simply is not adequate, but in terms of unemployment insurance surely we all recognize that what we need to aim at is a measure that will provide for the unemployed person insurance benefits as long as he is unemployed. The opinion that after a certain period of time it is good for his soul in some way to have his benefits cut down to 80 per cent, and that later on it is good for those benefits to be cut out altogether, is something parliament should not stand for at all. Amongst other things it has the effect of depressing wages.
I feel strongly that ways and means should be found to maintain supplementary benefits at the full amount provided in the earlier part of the act. Let us not feel satisfied. I suggest to the Liberal members of the house, who are trying to get this measure through, that they will rue the day they were so enthusiastic about it. Just wait until July- their supporters back in their constituencies will use the language the hon. member for

Unemployment Insurance Vancouver East has used tonight and say that a hoax has been put over on the working people of the country. A measure of this kind will not be satisfactory until it is recognized that it is just as hard to keep body and soul together after the normal period is exhausted as it is during that period, that it is harder still to do so when the benefit has been cut to 80 per cent, and harder still when the benefit has been removed altogether. We have no option but to agree to the passing of this section. We would not for one moment agree to anything less but we certainly protest against it.
I do not know whether or not this might be a good place for the minister to answer the questions that he has promised to answer. I suggest it is because one of them is related to this section. We have asked two main questions. What will the increased rates, provided for away back in section 3, bring in by way of revenue? The other question is what will the payments made under clause 87C amount to for the current year? Perhaps the minister might be prepared to give that information now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I am watching the clock because my primary concern, as it is the concern of all hon. members, is to make sure that we can make these benefits available as soon as possible. My hon. friend says they are inadequate. He has used other words, but to the extent that they have any value in his judgment I am sure he wants to get them out as quickly as we can. That is why I purposely refrained from answering a lot of things that could easily have been answered.
That is not in accordance with the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is the reason why.
You said you did not have the information.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Let us keep our tempers under control.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: As the Secretary of State for External Affairs would say, it is time for a cup of tea..

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I told the house earlier, with the qualification I have mentioned, that we would endeavour to give the estimates the commission has had in arriving at the proposed formula. It is thought that we might be able to pay benefits if it were necessary, for instance, to 80,000 persons, and I am taking that figure of 80,000 as a fixed figure for the whole period of three months. The distribution would be approximately $34,320,000. Hon. members may call that a hoax, but it is a substantial sum of money.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Let me-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Let me finish so that we can get the full picture.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What period would that amount be for?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Here is the calculation. Let us assume that 2,750,000 insured persons will be called upon to contribute from July 1, 1950 to March 31, 1952, and take from that let us say 100,000 unemployed over the period, because the figure can only be hypothetical, the result would be a total list of contributors amounting to 2,650,000. In the period of twenty-one months at 25 cents per month the figure of 2,650,000 persons would result in an amount of $13,912,500. The employers' contribution would be the same. The government's contribution would be $5,565,000, and the total would be $33,400,000. As must be obvious, these are rough figures. They can only be estimates, and it is not an easy thing to estimate. This is a novel experiment. Payments will be for seven and a half months or thirty-three weeks during the period. The payment to a person for benefits during all that period would be $429 if his rate was $13 per week, and if it was necessary, as I said at the outset, to pay benefits to 80,000 persons for the whole period it would cost roughly $34 million. These are figures that have got to be taken with reservations because it all depends on a whole set of contingencies that may or may not eventuate.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Just to get the matter clear, the $34,320,000 that the minister said it was estimated would be paid out to 80,000 people is for what period? Did he say seven and a half months?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes, seven and a half months.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In other words, those two figures are comparable. They are for the same period. The $34,320,000 to be paid out is for the month and a half this year, the three months in 1951 and the three months in 1952, and the $33,400,000 to be taken in is for the period beginning July 1 this year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: July 1.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: July 1 this year and carrying through to March 31, 1952. Therefore they are roughly comparable except that between now and July 1 of this year no additional payments are being brought in. Payments for twenty-one months just about equal the cost for two and one-half winter periods. We have now got what we tried to get' earlier in the day. The basis of the table is an attempt to secure an additional amount equal to what it is anticipated the government will pay out as supplementary benefits.

On section 20, clause 87D-Duration of supplementary benefit.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Would the minister explain paragraph (c)? I have in mind particularly the fact that as I read this clause the supplementary benefits for workers coming under it, that is people engaged in lumbering and logging, will not apply after March 31, 1951. In other words for that class there seems to be no permanent legislation respecting supplementary benefits, but legislation only for this winter and next winter.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Because they will then move into the insured class.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In other words they would get supplementary benefits, but they would get them under class 1?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
That is right.
Clause 87D agreed to.
On section 20, clause 87E-Suitable employment.

This refers to section 40 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, which deals with disqualification for neglecting an opportunity for work or failure to attend a course of instruction. In section 40 repeated reference is made to suitable employment, and they have gone some distance in defining that term. I do not say it is at all clear, but it is defined as being reasonable having regard to both the circumstances and the usual means of obtaining that employment. In clause 87E it appears that we have entirely departed from even that partial definition in section 40 of the act. Now an unemployed person is obliged to take any work which is deemed suitable; it even goes so far as to say he must accept any work he is able to perform. If these supplementary benefits were being given without additional contributions being required from the employees I could understand a more stringent application of this definition, but I can see no justification at all for such application in view of the fact that the employees are buying this additional protection. I am not going to say for a moment that I was ever satisfied with the administration of the act since 1940 with respect to this matter of suitable employment. Some day I should like to see a committee of this house make a thorough investigation into the administration of that section of the act. I do not want to take too much time, but I am registering a protest against this most severe application of the definition of the words "suitable employment".
Unemployment Insurance

Earlier in the afternoon I drew attention to this section as being one of these amendments having far-reaching consequences which, as far as I knew, had not been brought to the attention of the advisory committee or any of the large labour bodies. On this point I must associate myself with the remarks so ably made by the hon. member for Red Deer. The supplementary benefits under this act are being provided by an additional charge on those already contributing to the unemployment insurance fund, as well as by a new charge on teenagers, who are not contributing at the present time. If the insurance officer were a free agent in dealing with matters of this kind, and if he were a man of experience and understanding, he might be able to make a proper and reasonable decision as to what constituted suitable employment. But knowing the pressure that has been brought on unemployment insurance officers during the last few years to insist that people go to work in all kinds of employment that were not suitable at all, I am quite satisfied that the unemployment insurance commission administration is going to be in for a good deal of trouble if this section is adopted as it now stands. I would suggest to the minister that it be deleted and that the conditions governing these supplementary provisions be left as they are at present.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: So anxious am I to get this legislation through in order that benefits may go to unemployed persons at the earliest possible moment that I propose we drop this section..

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I shall not stand in the way of its being read a third time tonight, as is our right under the rules of the house. I am speaking only for myself, but I do want to say that if you ask for third reading tonight, you are doing it over my protest. The reason I am prepared to let the bill be called for third reading tonight is that there is a little bit in it that is good, and no one in the house is going to stand in the way of that little bit of good being made available. But I do protest as strongly as I can against the government coupling with the little bit that is good the objectionable features that we have protested against in this bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of fhe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Before the bill is read the third time, I wish to make it clear that in consenting to the reading of the bill for the third time now, to which consent must be given if it is to be done tonight, it is only for the purpose of making it possible to carry forward the payments that have been mentioned for which the bill provides. It is not to be taken that that implies approval of the way in which the bill is presented, the procedure which has been followed, which has given so little opportunity for adequate consideration of the details of the bill; nor is it in any way to be taken as approval of those parts of the bill to which objection has already been made, and to which there is a continuing objection on our part. I simply place that on record because I do agree that, with whatever limitations there are, it is desirable that the payments the government is prepared to provide, under such limitations as they impose, should go forward on March 1.

1
am not going to hold up the bill at all, nor am I going to say verv much. This afternoon I mentioned what I considered to be the government's-I used language this afternoon which you, sir, made me withdraw, so I shall leave it at that. The ordinary procedure of business in this house requires co-operation between the government and the opposition groups. 1 understand that this measure was simply to make provision for supplementary assistance to persons who are unemployed for long periods of time and have exhausted their unemployment benefits. To bring before us almost a complete review or overhaul of the Unemployment Insurance Act is something against which 1 must protest. It is something that would make me

extremely reluctant at any time in the future to assent to anything that this government brings down, until I see in black and white exactly what they want done.
I protest against it in the strongest possible terms. In passing this act, we have done some things today that should not have been done without consultation in a committee, where those concerned could make representations. It is just an insult to the members of this house to bring a complicated bill of this kind before them on such short notice. Even the government sponsors did not understand the bill.

I feel that the protests that have been made by the three hon. members who have spoken on the third reading of this bill are well made. My observation has been that since 1945, on all too numerous occasions, the government have brought measures before us with what they claimed was a limited time for consideration. They have pleaded, as the hon. minister pleaded tonight with tears in his voice, that we shut up and let the bill pass. I am serving notice on the minister and on the government not to ask us at any time to give carte blanche for the passage of bills of this kind or for rushing bills of this kind through.
In common with the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), I am going to see what is in a bill before I give my consent. I just want to say that I am not going to delay the third reading tonight. If I did the right thing for the people of this country, I would. It is a disgrace the way that sort of thing has been handled in this house during the past five years that I have been here. This is the end of it.
You would deprive the 70,000 boys of their money.
I may tell my quick-tempered friend over here that he does not know what he is talking about.
Don't I? I know better than you do.
The thing for the hon. member to do is to keep quiet.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Enough has been said, but the statements of the member for Mackenzie (Mr. Ferrie) prompt me to get to my feet again. He keeps talking about the people who
Unemployment Insurance might have been deprived had we continued our protests against the small benefits that are going out. We are letting the bill go through because of the small benefits, but let it be understood that the provisions for higher payments into the fund will come into effect on July 1, so next summer when the youngsters in his constituency and elsewhere find that they have to start contributing 18 cents a week to this scheme when they are making less than $5.40, when they come to him to complain, let him nor any other Liberal not pass the buck to those of us who have opposed the objectionable features in this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: In spite of what the hon. gentlemen have said, I simply want to thank the house for its co-operation on this measure. With regard to the misunderstandings and the reference to agreements, I only say to those who have made those statements that I indicated clearly this afternoon what I understood the situation to be. I do want to say that this measure, important as it is, was prepared as a result of careful consideration prior to its introduction here, and it was passed as a result of careful consideration here today. It is a measure of great consequence, and it is because of that that I thank the house and hon. members for their co-operation.

speakerposition: topic
Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On Monday we shall continue the debate on the address. I was astounded tonight to hear what was said before the passing of this bill. During last session I had the honour of leading this side of the house for the government, and I should like hon. members to know that I do not think anything was done to try to put anything over the opposition. I have been reading over what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said the other night. I did not attend the meetings with the leaders of the opposition, and I cannot say what happened there; but I can assure the house that anything I can do to co-operate with the opposition during the session I shall do with pleasure.
